sources.title: The Work of Transitions
sources.quote: are still immature, making it harder to switch focus between activities ... suggest a timer (sand timers work best) to help young children know how long they have left ... is more effective than yelling from the other room! ... transitions like the morning or bedtime routine can be made into a simple visual chart
sources.supports: Young children's executive function skills are still immature, which makes switching focus harder; a sand timer shows how much time is left; getting close and making eye contact works better than calling from another room.

sources.title: Activity changes for kids: behaviour tips
sources.publisher: Raising Children Network (Australia; last updated or reviewed 01-10-2024)
sources.quote: Children can accept change better when they know it’s coming. ... Give your child some warning about activity changes that are coming up. For example, ‘Desi, you have 5 more minutes to play. Then it will be time to go home’, or ‘Desi, one more go on the slide and then we’re going home’. ... Avoid giving your child a choice about an activity change if there isn’t really a choice. For example, when you say, ‘Orla, would you like to pack up those toys now?’ you suggest a choice. Instead you could say, ‘Orla, please start packing up those toys now’. ... Link something your child doesn’t want to do with something that they like. For example, ‘First we clean up the toys, and then we have a snack’. ... Choose your timing. If you can, stop one thing and start another during a natural break in your child’s activity. ... Give your child a choice about things that are part of the activity change. For example, ‘Evan, we have to go in the car in a minute. You can take one toy with you. Which one will it be?’ ... Limit options. For example, let your child choose between 2 different t-shirts, but not all the t-shirts in the drawer. ... Try making activity change fun. For example, ‘Can you march like a soldier to the car?’ ... Point out good things your child can look forward to after the change. ... It’s natural for your child to be disappointed about having to stop an activity that they’re enjoying. ... ‘I know you feel frustrated that you didn’t have time to play another game’. ... Role-play changes in activities, and talk with your child about how they might go.
sources.supports: Warn before a change; tie it to what comes next; take a natural break; no fake choices, real limited choices about other things; make it fun; disappointment is natural and can be named; role-play the change.

sources.title: Preschool Prep: Helping Toddlers Prepare for Preschool
sources.quote: Talk about the story and how the characters are feeling.
sources.supports: Reading books about an upcoming change and talking about how the characters feel. (Written for starting preschool; we apply the idea of a story as a way to talk about a hard change, as an analogy.)

claims.wording_he: קשה לי לעצור באמצע ואני לא יודע כמה זמן נשאר
claims.supports: Young children's ability to switch focus is still immature (Mount Sinai); the child's first-person wording is ours.
Warn before the change and name what happens next, as in the Raising Children Network example of 5 more minutes to play.
Give a choice about things that are part of the change, such as taking one toy with you.

Role-playing a hard change and talking about how the characters feel are both recommended; ZERO TO THREE's page is about starting preschool, so it is used as an analogy. That the story is personalised, with the child as the hero, is our wording.
The book behind the comment link: the child's name is in the text and the child stars in every illustration (live site, 2026-10-11). No brand or title on the slide.

sources.title: Activity changes for kids: behaviour tips
sources.publisher: Raising Children Network (Australia; last updated or reviewed 01-10-2024)
sources.quote: Children can accept change better when they know it’s coming. ... Give your child some warning about activity changes that are coming up. For example, ‘Desi, you have 5 more minutes to play. Then it will be time to go home’, or ‘Desi, one more go on the slide and then we’re going home’. ... Avoid giving your child a choice about an activity change if there isn’t really a choice. For example, when you say, ‘Orla, would you like to pack up those toys now?’ you suggest a choice. Instead you could say, ‘Orla, please start packing up those toys now’. ... Link something your child doesn’t want to do with something that they like. For example, ‘First we clean up the toys, and then we have a snack’. ... Choose your timing. If you can, stop one thing and start another during a natural break in your child’s activity. ... Give your child a choice about things that are part of the activity change. For example, ‘Evan, we have to go in the car in a minute. You can take one toy with you. Which one will it be?’ ... Limit options. For example, let your child choose between 2 different t-shirts, but not all the t-shirts in the drawer. ... Try making activity change fun. For example, ‘Can you march like a soldier to the car?’ ... Point out good things your child can look forward to after the change. ... It’s natural for your child to be disappointed about having to stop an activity that they’re enjoying. ... ‘I know you feel frustrated that you didn’t have time to play another game’. ... Role-play changes in activities, and talk with your child about how they might go.

sources.title: The Work of Transitions
sources.quote: are still immature, making it harder to switch focus between activities ... suggest a timer (sand timers work best) to help young children know how long they have left ... is more effective than yelling from the other room! ... transitions like the morning or bedtime routine can be made into a simple visual chart
sources.supports: Young children's executive function skills are still immature, which makes switching focus harder; a sand timer shows how much time is left; getting close and making eye contact works better than calling from another room.

sources.title: Activity changes for kids: behaviour tips
sources.publisher: Raising Children Network (Australia; last updated or reviewed 01-10-2024)
sources.quote: Children can accept change better when they know it’s coming. ... Give your child some warning about activity changes that are coming up. For example, ‘Desi, you have 5 more minutes to play. Then it will be time to go home’, or ‘Desi, one more go on the slide and then we’re going home’. ... Avoid giving your child a choice about an activity change if there isn’t really a choice. For example, when you say, ‘Orla, would you like to pack up those toys now?’ you suggest a choice. Instead you could say, ‘Orla, please start packing up those toys now’. ... Link something your child doesn’t want to do with something that they like. For example, ‘First we clean up the toys, and then we have a snack’. ... Choose your timing. If you can, stop one thing and start another during a natural break in your child’s activity. ... Give your child a choice about things that are part of the activity change. For example, ‘Evan, we have to go in the car in a minute. You can take one toy with you. Which one will it be?’ ... Limit options. For example, let your child choose between 2 different t-shirts, but not all the t-shirts in the drawer. ... Try making activity change fun. For example, ‘Can you march like a soldier to the car?’ ... Point out good things your child can look forward to after the change. ... It’s natural for your child to be disappointed about having to stop an activity that they’re enjoying. ... ‘I know you feel frustrated that you didn’t have time to play another game’. ... Role-play changes in activities, and talk with your child about how they might go.
sources.supports: Warn before a change; tie it to what comes next; take a natural break; no fake choices, real limited choices about other things; make it fun; disappointment is natural and can be named; role-play the change.

sources.title: How Can We Help Kids With Transitions?
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (Katherine Martinelli; last updated September 15, 2025)
sources.quote: give a time frame and description of what will happen along with countdowns ... make a connection with the child to ensure that you have their attention ... Dr. Rosenthal suggests doing a role-play in which you practice moving from activity to activity ... In the morning you might lay out what the day is going to look like.
sources.supports: A time frame and countdown before a transition; get the child's attention first; role-play moving between activities; preview the day.
